title: Why the Seven New NFL Stadiums Being Built Are Mostly Domed

vocab.articleQuote: The older domes from the 1960s and ’70s were essentially concrete roofs—opaque, dark, no natural light.
vocab.inContext: The old stadium roofs were solid concrete that let no light through, so being inside felt like sitting in a giant parking garage. The new roofs are the opposite — sunlight filters right through them.
vocab.meaning: Not letting light pass through; impossible to see through. The opposite of transparent (like clear glass).
examples: I covered my notebook with opaque tape so nobody could read the answers underneath.
Unlike a clear water bottle, my opaque one hides how much juice I have left.

vocab.articleQuote: A few things are converging at once.
vocab.inContext: Several separate forces — concert money, Super Bowl rules, and television deals — are all coming together at the same time, and together they push teams to build roofs.
vocab.meaning: To come together toward the same point, or to happen at the same time from different directions.
examples: After the final buzzer, fans converged on the court from every corner of the gym.
Three hallways converge at the cafeteria, which is why it gets so crowded at lunch.

vocab.articleQuote: It’s what I’d call the declining public-share paradox.
vocab.inContext: Taxpayers now pay a smaller SHARE of each stadium's cost than they used to — yet they hand over more actual dollars than ever, because the stadiums have gotten so much more expensive. Two facts that seem to clash, both true.
vocab.meaning: A statement or situation that seems to contradict itself, but turns out to be true anyway.
examples: It's a paradox that the busiest kid in school somehow always finishes homework first.
"The more you learn, the more you realize how much you don't know" is a famous paradox.

concepts.name: Cost per use
concepts.articleQuote: A team plays nine or so home games a year—that’s 10 days of use out of 365.
concepts.meaning:
Here's a smart way to think about any expensive thing: don't ask "how much does it cost?" — ask "how much does it cost each time I use it?" A $100 pair of cleats you wear twice costs $50 per wear. A $100 pair you wear a hundred times costs $1 per wear. Same price tag, completely different deal.

Now look at an NFL stadium the same way. It costs around $3 billion, and the football team plays there only about 10 days a year. That's a gigantic machine sitting dark and empty 355 days out of 365 — a terrible cost per use. But put a roof on it, and suddenly it can host concerts, conventions, and big events all year long, in any weather. More days of use makes every single day cheaper. That — more than anything about football itself — is why almost every new stadium is getting a dome.

You can use this trick on your own money. Before buying something expensive, guess honestly how many times you'll really use it, then divide. It's how you tell a true bargain from a very fancy dust collector.

concepts.name: The substitution effect
concepts.articleQuote: When a family spends $300 at a game, that’s $300 they don’t spend at a local restaurant or bowling alley; there’s no new economic activity, just what we economists call “substitution.”
concepts.meaning:
Suppose a new candy store opens near your school and you spend your $10 allowance there. Did your town just get $10 richer? No — that's $10 you now DIDN'T spend at the pizza place next door. Your money didn't grow; it just moved. Economists call this substitution: one kind of spending replacing another.

This is the secret to judging big promises like "a new stadium will boost the city's economy!" Most of the money families spend at a game is money they would have spent anyway — on movies, restaurants, or bowling — somewhere else in the same town. The stadium's cash registers fill up while other businesses' registers empty out a little, and the town as a whole barely changes. That's why economists who study stadiums keep finding that they don't create the boom that gets promised.

New wealth shows up only when the spending comes from OUTSIDE — visitors who wouldn't have come otherwise — or when something genuinely new gets made. So next time someone says a big project will "bring in money," ask the substitution question: is this new money, or old money in a new place?

quiz.question: According to the article, why are almost all the new NFL stadiums being built with roofs?
options: Players complained that sunshine made it hard to catch the ball
An enclosed stadium can earn money all year from concerts and events, not just from about 10 football days
Open-air stadiums are no longer allowed by league rules
Roofs help the grass on the field grow better
quiz.explanation: A team uses its stadium only about 10 days a year, so a roof lets the building earn money on the other 355 days with concerts, conventions, and other events.

quiz.question: Why do television networks prefer games in enclosed stadiums?
options: The stadium lights make players look better on camera
Indoor crowds cheer more loudly
A game can't be delayed or called off by weather, so the broadcast they paid for is guaranteed to happen
Domes have more room for camera crews
quiz.explanation: Most NFL money comes from TV deals, and networks want certainty that a scheduled game will actually be played on time.

quiz.question: A family spends $300 at a stadium instead of at local restaurants and the bowling alley. What does the article say this means for the city's economy?
options: The city gains $300 of brand-new wealth
The money mostly just moved from one business to another, so the city as a whole barely gains
The city loses the whole $300
The money doubles because stadiums attract more spending
quiz.explanation: That's the substitution effect — spending that moves from one place to another isn't new economic activity.

quiz.question: You have $60 to spend on either a costume you'll wear once or a backpack you'll use every school day for a year. Using "cost per use," which is the better deal?
options: The costume, because one big moment matters most
They're exactly equal, because both cost $60
Neither — cost per use only applies to buildings
The backpack — spread over about 180 school days, it costs only pennies per use
quiz.explanation: Dividing the price by the number of uses shows the backpack costs about 33 cents per day, while the costume costs $60 for a single wear.

quiz.question: The article calls it a "paradox" that taxpayers pay a smaller SHARE of stadium costs than before, yet more DOLLARS than ever. Why is that a paradox?
options: Because one of the two facts must be false
Because the two facts seem to contradict each other, and yet both are true
Because paradoxes only happen with percentages
Because taxpayers don't actually pay for stadiums
quiz.explanation: A paradox seems self-contradictory but is true — a smaller slice of a much bigger pie can still be more pie.
